Husayn Muruwwa was born in 1910, according to his official papers, though he himself believed that he was probably born in 1908. He was born in the village of Hadatha, in the Bint Jbeil district of southern Lebanon. He received his early education in Bint Jbeil and Nabatieh.
In 1924, he travelled to Iraq to study religious sciences, Arabic language, and Arabic literature at the religious college in Najaf. He completed his studies there in 1938.

In 1948, he took an active part—as a political participant, journalist, and writer—in Iraq’s national popular uprising known as the Wathba, which brought down the colonial British Portsmouth Treaty with the Iraqi monarchy. After the conservative reaction that followed, Nuri al-Said—described here as “Britain’s man in Iraq”—returned to power. In May 1949, he ordered Husayn Muruwwa to be expelled from Iraq. Muruwwa returned to Lebanon in June of that year.

Back in Lebanon, he began writing his well-known daily column, “With the Caravan,” for the newspaper al-Hayat. He also helped found the left-wing magazine al-Thaqafa al-Wataniyya and worked on its editorial staff from 1952 until it ceased publication as a literary and intellectual magazine in 1959. From the 1950s onward, he also contributed to the magazine al-Tariq, and from the late 1960s until the day of his assassination he oversaw its editorial work. He also wrote for the newspapers al-Nidaʾ and al-Akhbar.

His books, in order of publication, include: With the Caravan (articles), 1952; Literary Questions (studies in literary criticism), 1956; The Iraqi Revolution (a study in modern history), 1985; Critical Studies in the Light of the Critical Method (literary criticism); Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy (a foundational work in the Marxist study of the Arab philosophical heritage, in two volumes), 1978; Studies in Islam (with Maḥmūd Amīn al-ʿĀlim, Muḥammad Dakrūb, and Samīr Saʿd), 1978; On Heritage and Islamic Law (studies), 1983; New Titles for Old Faces (studies on heritage and the thought of the Arab Renaissance), 1984; Our Heritage: How Should We Understand It? (studies on Arab heritage), 1986; and Studies in Thought and Literature (literary criticism, published after his assassination), 1993. He also left a large number of studies, research papers, and articles across many fields of knowledge. These were being collected and organized for publication in separate volumes.
Husayn Muruwwa was assassinated in his home on 17 February 1987. He was 79 years old.

Historians disagree about the dates of al-Kindī’s birth and death. Among modern scholars, some (Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq and Abū Rīda) say that he died in 252 AH/866 CE; others (Henry Corbin and Nallino) put his death in 260 AH/873 CE; and Massignon gives the date as 246 AH/860 CE. See Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Three Muslim Sages, p. 165.↩︎

Al-Kindī was known in Latin as Alkindus. One of the earliest Orientalists to translate his works into Latin was Gerard of Cremona (1114–1187). See Korkis ʿAwwād, Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī: His Life and Works, Baghdad, 1962, p. 13.↩︎
See Richard Walzer, Islamic Philosophy and Its Place in Human Thought, Dār al-ʿIlm lil-Malāyīn, Beirut, 1958, translated by Muḥammad Tawfīq Ḥusayn, p. 27.↩︎

About forty years ago, virtually all we knew of al-Kindī came from reports preserved by historians and from incomplete excerpts of works whose full texts were unknown to us. This changed when the German Orientalist Ritter discovered a number of al-Kindī’s treatises in the Hagia Sophia Library in Istanbul and published them with the Orientalist Plessner in the Czechoslovak Orientalist journal in 1932. From then on, al-Kindī’s works began to appear in scholarly editions. Dr. Aḥmad Fuʾād al-Ahwānī in Cairo published Al-Kindī’s Book to al-Muʿtaṣim on First Philosophy in 1948. Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda, also in Cairo, published Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises in two volumes containing twenty-five treatises between 1950 and 1953. Dr. Fayṣal Badawī in Iraq published Al-Kindī’s Treatise on the Making of Swords in 1962. Yūsuf Zakariyyā and Maḥmūd Aḥmad al-Ḥifnī worked with several Orientalists on scholarly editions of al-Kindī’s writings on music. Yūsuf Yaʿqūb Maskūnī in Baghdad published Al-Kindī’s Treatise on the Production of Weather. Orientalists including Ritter and Karl Garbers published al-Kindī’s work on the chemistry of perfume and sublimation, while Neheimer and others also took part in this work. Yet everything by al-Kindī that has so far been identified and published still represents only a very small part of the total body of work described by Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Qifṭī, Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, and Qāḍī Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī. Ibn al-Nadīm lists 241 books and treatises by al-Kindī (The Fihrist, Leipzig, p. 255); Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa lists 281 (Classes of Physicians, Cairo, p. 29); and al-Qifṭī lists 228 (History of the Sages, Leipzig, p. 368). Qāḍī Ṣāʿid says that al-Kindī had more than fifty famous works in most branches of knowledge, ranging from long books to short treatises (Classes of Nations, Beirut, p. 52). What is actually available to readers today, however, amounts to no more than 42 printed works, 30 works still surviving in manuscript in libraries around the world, and 34 works translated into Latin, English, French, Italian, German, and Persian. Some of these translations survive even though their Arabic originals are lost. See Father Richard Joseph McCarthy, S.J., Works Attributed to the Philosopher of the Arabs, Baghdad, 1962.↩︎
Carl Brockelmann, History of the Islamic Peoples, Arabic edition, Beirut, vol. 2, p. 39.↩︎

A subject-based catalogue of al-Kindī’s writings compiled by Father Richard Joseph McCarthy, S.J. (previously cited source, pp. 115–118) suggests the following totals: 14 works on arithmetic; 21 on geometry and surveying; 8 on dimensions; 12 on spheres; 4 on optics; 15 on music; about 45 on astronomy and meteorological phenomena; about 43 on astrology; 5 on geography; about 36 on medicine; 117 on philosophy, including general treatises, logic, natural philosophy, metaphysics, psychology, ethics, and politics; 20 on kalām and disputation; and 15 on chemistry, including perfume-making, swords, gems and stones, and mirrors. This is apart from about 31 miscellaneous works.↩︎

Roger Bacon, for example, ranked al-Kindī and al-Ḥasan ibn al-Haytham in the first rank alongside Ptolemy (Qadrī Ṭūqān, Science among the Arabs, p. 104). Al-Bīrūnī says that in the science of gems and stones he knew no work other than al-Kindī’s book on gems and related substances, and praises al-Kindī’s originality in every field he touched, calling him a leader among modern scholars and a model for researchers (al-Bīrūnī, The Book of Precious Stones, Hyderabad ed., 1355 AH, pp. 31–32).↩︎

Henry Corbin denies that al-Kindī translated ancient texts (History of Islamic Philosophy, p. 236), but Arab historians say that he did. Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa (Classes of Physicians, vol. 1, p. 207) reports that Abū Maʿshar wrote in his Memoirs for Shādhān: “The four master translators are Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī, Thābit ibn Qurra, and ʿUmar ibn al-Farrukhān al-Ṭabarī.” Sulaymān ibn Ḥassān, the Andalusian physician known as Ibn Juljul (fourth century AH), says that al-Kindī “translated many works of philosophy, clarified what was difficult in them, and summarized what was obscure and hard to understand” (Classes of Physicians and Sages, ed. Fuʾād Sayyid, Cairo, 1955, pp. 73–74). Al-Qifṭī also quotes this statement from Ibn Juljul (Accounts of the Sages, p. 241). See ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī, The Role of the Arabs in the Formation of European Thought. Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq (The Philosopher of the Arabs and the Second Teacher, Cairo, 1945, p. 21) confirms that al-Kindī learned Greek. Massignon likewise says of al-Kindī: “He deserves credit for revising a number of Arabic translations of Greek philosophical works” (Massignon, Collection of Unpublished Texts from the History of Sufism in Islam, Paris, 1929, in French).↩︎

Ẓahīr al-Dīn al-Bayhaqī says in History of the Sages (Damascus ed., 1946, p. 41) that al-Muʿtaṣim “attached al-Kindī to his court; he was tutor to al-Muʿtaṣim’s son, and he wrote treatises to Aḥmad ibn al-Muʿtaṣim.” Ibn Nubāta al-Miṣrī writes (Sarḥ al-ʿUyūn fī Sharḥ Risālat Ibn Zaydūn, Būlāq ed., 1278 AH, p. 123): “The reign of al-Muʿtaṣim was adorned by him”—that is, by al-Kindī—“and by his writings.”↩︎

In introducing al-Kindī, Ibn Nubāta (previously cited source) says that he was “known in his time as the Philosopher of Islam.” Qāḍī Ṣāʿid (Classes of Nations, p. 52) says that no one in Islam except Yaʿqūb had become so famous among the public for the philosophical sciences that people simply called him “the philosopher.” Notice Ibn Nubāta’s words “in his time,” and Qāḍī Ṣāʿid’s phrase “in Islam.” Both point to the title having been used in al-Kindī’s own age. The other sources indicate the same thing.↩︎

See, for example, De Boer, History of Philosophy in Islam, p. 19, and Rom Landau, who says in discussing al-Kindī’s philosophy that he was “famous as the Philosopher of the Arabs because of his unmistakably Arab ancestry” (Islam and the Arabs, p. 217). Compare the previous note, where Ibn Nubāta calls al-Kindī “the Philosopher of Islam,” and where Ṣāʿid says “in Islam,” not “among the Arabs.” This clearly shows that the title “Philosopher of the Arabs” does not refer to ancestry. See Majid Fakhry, Al-Kindī and Socrates, p. 23.↩︎

For al-Kindī, “rational knowledge” belongs to the human being’s “rational existence.” He divides human existence into sensory existence and rational existence, and he regards rational existence as the true form of existence. Sensory existence, by contrast, “is not stable, because what it encounters passes away, flows, and changes.” In al-Kindī’s system, rational existence is connected with universals, by which he means genera and species (previously cited source, pp. 84–85). The Platonic influence is obvious in his distinction between rational existence as “true” and sensory existence as “unstable.”↩︎

Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq regards this division of knowledge in al-Kindī as one of the clearest signs of his philosophical importance, calling it “a mark of genius and the basis of his lasting name in history.” He gives this reason: al-Kindī “was the first to divide philosophy into three sciences: theology, mathematics, and natural science (...). This way of understanding philosophy and dividing it according to subject matter therefore gave Islamic philosophy its direction from the very beginning” (M. ʿAbd al-Rāziq, The Philosopher of the Arabs and the Second Teacher, Cairo, 1945, pp. 45–46). See al-Kindī’s Treatise on the Intellect and Treatise on the Nature of Sleep and Dreams, in Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, ed. Abū Rīda, Cairo, 1950, vol. 1.↩︎
Al-Kindī’s Book to al-Muʿtaṣim on First Philosophy, al-Ahwānī ed., p. 82.↩︎

In al-Kindī’s philosophical terminology, the “first cause” means God. See al-Kindī’s Treatise Explaining the Efficient Cause, in Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, edited and published by Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda, Cairo, 1950, vol. 1, p. 219. The term suggests a connection with Aristotle’s “first cause.” Al-Kindī also uses other philosophical terms for God, including “the First Truth,” “the true, first, complete agent,” “the Absolute,” and “the Eternal.” See Al-Kindī’s Treatise on First Philosophy and Al-Kindī’s Treatise on the True, First, Complete Agent, in the same source. The phrase “the true, first, complete agent” suggests the influence of the Neoplatonic theory of emanation. It points to a series of intermediaries in creation, each of which al-Kindī treats only figuratively as an agent—secondary and incomplete. God alone is the true, first, complete agent.↩︎

We can see this in his discussion of God through the concepts on which he built his complete theory of intellect and definitions, until he arrives at the concept of the “first cause” and the science devoted to it, which he calls “first philosophy” in keeping with the Aristotelian method. See the opening of Al-Kindī’s Treatise on First Philosophy, previously cited source.↩︎
